templates.pattern: Two resistors of resistance [R1] Ω and [R2] Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the combined resistance of the parallel combination in ohms.
templates.explanation:
Parallel resistance:
1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
R = R₁ × R₂ ÷ (R₁ + R₂)
= [R1] × [R2] ÷ ([R1] + [R2])
= [R1*R2] ÷ [R1+R2]
= [RESULT] Ω

The combined resistance of a parallel combination is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

templates.pattern: In a series circuit a battery of EMF [EMF] V drives a current of [I] A through three resistors with potential differences of [V1] V, [V2] V and [V3] V across them. Calculate the potential difference across the third resistor in volts.
templates.explanation:
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law: sum of all potential differences = EMF
EMF = V₁ + V₂ + V₃
V₃ = EMF − V₁ − V₂
= [EMF] − [V1] − [V2]
= [RESULT] V

In a series circuit the sum of all potential differences across components equals the EMF of the source.

templates.pattern: A wire of resistivity [RHO] × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m has a length of [L] m and a cross-sectional area of [A] mm². Calculate the resistance of the wire in ohms.
templates.explanation:
Resistance = resistivity × length ÷ area
= R = ρL ÷ A
= ([RHO] × 10⁻⁸ × [L]) ÷ ([A] × 10⁻⁶)
= [RHO] × [L] ÷ ([A] × 100)
= [RESULT] Ω

Resistivity is a property of the material. A longer thinner wire has greater resistance.

templates.pattern: A battery has an EMF of [EMF] V and an internal resistance of [r] Ω. A current of [I] A flows through the circuit. Calculate the terminal potential difference of the battery in volts.
templates.explanation:
Terminal pd = EMF − I × r
= [EMF] − [I] × [r]
= [EMF] − [I*r]
= [RESULT] V

The terminal voltage is always less than the EMF when current flows. The difference is the voltage lost across the internal resistance — called the lost volts.

templates.pattern: A battery has an EMF of [EMF] V and delivers a current of [I] A. The terminal voltage is [V] V. Calculate the internal resistance of the battery in ohms.
templates.explanation:
Internal resistance r = (EMF − V) ÷ I
= ([EMF] − [V]) ÷ [I]
= [I*r] ÷ [I]
= [RESULT] Ω

Internal resistance causes the terminal voltage to drop when current flows. A battery with high internal resistance cannot deliver large currents efficiently.

templates.pattern: A transformer has [N1] turns on the primary coil and [N2] turns on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is [V1] V. Calculate the secondary voltage in volts.
templates.explanation:
Transformer equation: V₂ ÷ V₁ = N₂ ÷ N₁
V₂ = V₁ × N₂ ÷ N₁
= [V1] × [N2] ÷ [N1]
= [RESULT] V

A step-up transformer has more secondary turns and increases voltage. A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns and decreases voltage.

templates.pattern: A transformer has [N1] turns on the primary and [N2] turns on the secondary. The primary current is [I1] A. Calculate the secondary current in amperes. (Assume 100% efficiency)
templates.explanation:
For an ideal transformer: I₂ = I₁ × N₁ ÷ N₂
= [I1] × [N1] ÷ [N2]
= [RESULT] A

When a transformer steps up voltage it steps down current proportionally. This conserves power since P = VI.

templates.pattern: A charge of [Q] C is accelerated through a potential difference of [V] V. Calculate the electrical energy gained by the charge in joules.
templates.explanation:
Electrical Energy = Charge × Potential Difference
= E = QV
= [Q] × [V]
= [RESULT] J

This formula shows that energy is transferred when charge moves through a potential difference. It is the basis of how batteries and power supplies transfer energy to circuits.

templates.pattern: A straight conductor of length [L] m carries a current of [I] A perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density [B] T. Calculate the force on the conductor in newtons.
templates.explanation:
Force on conductor = BIL
= [B] × [I] × [L]
= [RESULT] N

This force is the basis of electric motors. The direction of the force is given by Fleming's Left Hand Rule. Maximum force occurs when the conductor is perpendicular to the field.

templates.pattern: A magnetic field of flux density [B] T passes perpendicularly through an area of [A] m². Calculate the magnetic flux through the area in webers.
templates.explanation:
Magnetic flux Φ = B × A
= [B] × [A]
= [RESULT] Wb

Magnetic flux measures the total magnetic field passing through an area. The weber (Wb) is the unit of magnetic flux. 1 Wb = 1 T·m².
